summary: Beyond the Hotspots is Team The Kernel’s interactive burning-activity calendar and 3D fire map for a selected region of Brazil’s Pantanal. We used NASA FIRMS observations to compare Terra and Aqua MODIS with Suomi NPP VIIRS, which differ in resolution, sensitivity, and sampling. We counted activity on a shared 2 km grid and estimated MODIS totals on the VIIRS scale for the period with records from both sensors. Across 120 months outside coefficient fitting, monthly weighted absolute error against observed Suomi NPP VIIRS fell from 44.48% for unadjusted MODIS to 9.94% after harmonization. This measures retrospective satellite agreement. The calendar covers February 2003 to January 2026 and shows observed MODIS before February 2012. Fire managers and researchers can compare months with their historical norms, explore where the sensors detected activity, and download results for further analysis.
details:
What we built

Beyond the Hotspots pairs a burning-activity calendar with a 3D fire map for a study area within Brazil’s Pantanal, from 58°W to 56°W and 19.5°S to 17°S. Terra and Aqua MODIS use nominal 1 km active-fire pixels, and Suomi NPP VIIRS uses nominal 375 m pixels. Differences in resolution, sensitivity, and overpass timing can make the same month look very different across the two records. A change of sensor can therefore look like a change in burning activity.

The dashboard spans 276 months from February 2003 to January 2026. Its calendar shows observed MODIS before February 2012 and includes VIIRS-scale estimates during the paired period. Users can select observed MODIS across the full record, switch between the available series, and open a month to compare the totals. The “vs. usual” view compares each month with the median for that calendar month within the selected series. This gives fire managers and researchers a historical reference for identifying unusually active periods. The dashboard also provides a timeline, an error-by-season chart, and CSV downloads.

The dashboard’s Yearly view compares observed MODIS activity with the median for the same calendar month. September 2020 is outlined at 6.6 times the September median.

How we harmonized the records

We filtered NASA FIRMS records to retain presumed vegetation-fire detections inside the study area. We kept MODIS detections with confidence of at least 30 and VIIRS detections with nominal or high confidence. We converted acquisition times to historical local dates in America/Cuiaba and put both sensors on a shared 2 km × 2 km equal-area grid. One active cell-day is one grid cell with at least one qualifying detection on one local day. Terra and Aqua detections in the same cell on the same day count once in the combined MODIS total.

The released model averages two estimates equally. The first uses a 1.84× multiplier fitted on complete weeks. The second weights monthly MODIS cell-days by three fire radiative power bands, using the maximum power recorded in each cell-day. The bands are below 10 MW, 10 to below 50 MW, and 50 MW or more. Both components minimize absolute error against observed Suomi NPP VIIRS using data from February 2013 through January 2017. The power bands let the adjustment respond to the mix of weaker and stronger detections in a month.

Report Figure 1. The workflow filters the archived detections, counts active cell-days on a shared grid, fits two calibrations, and averages their estimates.

WORKED EXAMPLE

September 2020 in the Pantanal

September 2020 had the highest observed MODIS activity in our 276-month record. MODIS recorded 4,058 active cell-days, about 6.6 times the dashboard’s September median of 615 cell-days. That median uses all 23 Septembers from 2003 through 2025, including 2020.

For the same month, Suomi NPP VIIRS recorded 7,108 cell-days. Applying the 1.84× multiplier alone gives 7,466.72 cell-days. The final ensemble estimates 7,136.12 cell-days.

Switching the 3D fire map to Both shows where the sensors recorded activity during the month. The legend counts distinct cells on the globe’s approximate display grid. A cell marked “Both” had a detection from each sensor at some point that month. The three summary cards show the dashboard’s monthly cell-day totals.

September 2020 in Both mode. Gold marks 1,687 display cells detected by both sensors, cyan marks 529 VIIRS-only cells, and magenta marks 91 MODIS-only cells. The panel above the legend shows monthly cell-day totals.

Fire data from NASA FIRMS. Imagery from Esri, Vantor (shown as Maxar in the app), Earthstar Geographics, and the GIS User Community. Place labels from Esri, HERE, Garmin, © OpenStreetMap contributors, and the GIS User Community. Terrain from Mapzen/AWS Terrain Tiles, with global elevation data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey and NOAA.

Validation

How we tested agreement

Across 120 months outside coefficient fitting, monthly weighted absolute error against observed Suomi NPP VIIRS was 44.48% for unadjusted MODIS, 11.51% for the fixed multiplier, and 9.94% for the final ensemble. We calculated this measure by dividing the sum of absolute monthly errors by the total observed VIIRS cell-days in those same months.

The evaluation periods were examined during development. The result measures retrospective satellite agreement for totals across the study area. The dashboard uses the four-season fit described above. A separate full-overlap refit uses all 14 paired seasons and has its own coefficients and evaluation results.

Report Figure 3. The same 120 months outside coefficient fitting are shown for unadjusted MODIS, the 1.84× multiplier, and the final ensemble. Both axes are in cell-days per month. The dashed lines mark equal totals.

Closing

Tools and limitations

We processed the archives in Python notebooks using pandas, NumPy, and pyproj, and fitted the power-band model with SciPy. We built the browser tools with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The companion globe uses MapLibre GL JS, and both tools are hosted on Vercel.

The calibration estimates detected activity for the full study rectangle. Estimating burned area, identifying individual fire incidents, or applying the model to a different area would require separate evidence. Satellite observation coverage remains unverified. The globe displays observed detections on an approximate 0.02° grid with a fixed UTC−4 date convention. The dashboard analysis uses the equal-area grid and historical local dates described above.
